title: Microcadence survey: latency vs cost for stitch strategies (draft)
body:
PURPOSE:
Quick exploratory writeup of how "microcadence" (many tiny conversational turns with short idle gaps) trades latency for cost depending on stitch/prefetch strategies. This is a messy working doc — experimental notes + ascii charts + quick ops recommendations.

BACKGROUND / MOTIVATION:
- We see a growing workload pattern from a couple of customers: lots of short user messages (5–40 tokens) separated by 0.5–5s idle. Traditional session-oriented packing underuses slots; pure per-request serving pays high per-token overhead.
- Idea: stitch multiple micro-turns either on the client (bundle before send) or on the server (speculative prefetch + soft-stitch) to amortize fixed per-request token overhead. Need baseline metrics for latency impact vs unit cost.

EXPERIMENT SETUP (quick):
- Model: open-llm-13b-ish (quantized profile used in Dedicated pool).
- HW: A100-equivalent, 1 GPU per shard, session-slot model (typical Redwood Dedicated config).
- Workloads simulated:
  * micro-turn: 10 tokens prompt, 12 token generation, inter-turn gap 1s
  * burst micro: 3 turns in 3s (tight), sparse micro: 3 turns across 12s (looser cadence)
- Strategies compared:
  A) naive (each turn -> independent request)
  B) client-bundle (client collects turns up to 3 or 2s then sends as a single request)
  C) server-stitch (server receives first turn, speculatively warm / prefetch KV and holds slot for 500ms waiting for come-one-more; attempts to stitch subsequent turns into same execution if they arrive)
  D) partial-prefetch (server starts KV cache only, returns very-low-latency stub if no additional turns)
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency per-turn (end-to-end), cost per 1k turns (amortized GPU-seconds -> $), slot occupancy %, tail amplification factor (p99/p50).

RAW OBSERVATIONS (coarse numbers — bench harness output):
- naive:
  p50: 120ms, p95: 420ms, p99: 980ms, cost per 1k turns: $3.40
  slot occupancy: 12% (lots of idle between small requests)
- client-bundle (optimal bundling when available):
  p50: 180ms (per turn, because combined request adds marginal decode), p95: 520ms, p99: 1.1s, cost per 1k turns: $1.95
  slot occupancy: 38%
- server-stitch (500ms hold):
  p50: 140ms (for stitched turns that arrive within hold), p95: 610ms (tails include waits), p99: 1.5s, cost per 1k turns: $2.10
  slot occupancy: 29%
- partial-prefetch:
  p50: 125ms, p95: 465ms, p99: 1.05s, cost per 1k turns: $2.70
  slot occupancy: 18%

ASCII CHART: (per-turn latency CDF sketch; x-axis ms, markers p50/p95/p99)
- naive:  [ p50=120 | p95=420 | p99=980 ]
- client-bundle: [ p50=180 | p95=520 | p99=1100 ]
- server-stitch: [ p50=140 | p95=610 | p99=1500 ]
- partial-prefetch: [ p50=125 | p95=465 | p99=1050 ]

COST VS LATENCY TRADEOFFS (interpretation notes):
- Client-bundle gives the most cost savings at expense of predictable per-turn latency increase (since turns are explicitly batched). If the client can accept ~60ms extra p50, it's the cheapest.
- Server-stitch reduces cost (vs naive) without client changes, but introduces variable added latency for stitched-turns and a longer tail due to the hold-window. It also increases slot occupancy which can hurt multi-tenant fairness.
- Partial-prefetch looks like a sweet spot: small cost savings, minimal p50 increase, moderate tail. Works well when we can prefetch KV cheaply.

SIMPLE VISUAL (cost per 1k turns vs p95 latency):
- naive:   $3.40 @ p95 420ms
- client-bundle: $1.95 @ p95 520ms
- server-stitch: $2.10 @ p95 610ms
- partial-prefetch: $2.70 @ p95 465ms

NOTES / QUALIFIERS:
- numbers above are synthetic from local bench harness. Absolute dollars depend on GPU config, preemption, etc.
- Tail behavior for server-stitch is sensitive to hold-window and session churn. 500ms was chosen as midpoint; 200ms reduces tail but also reduces stitch-hit rate (and thus less cost benefit).
- Client-bundle depends on product UX; long holds on client to aggregate degrade interactivity. For messaging apps where users type multi-turn quickly it's fine; not for voice agents.

SAMPLE STITCH HIT RATES (from trace-replay):
- burst micro (tight cadence): stitch hit-rate ~72% at 500ms
- sparse micro (loose cadence): stitch hit-rate ~18% at 500ms
- hit-rate -> directly maps to cost reduction roughly linearly (approx)

OPERATIONAL CONCERNS / SAFETY:
- Holding slots increases exposure to noisy tenants. Need per-tenant stitch caps or a slot-reservation budget.
- Billing clarity: if turns are stitched on-server, how do we attribute tokens to customer invoices (we do, but need clear docs).
- SLAs: customers expecting strict p95 guarantees may need opt-out from server-stitch.

QUICK RECS (draft):
- Offer server-side partial-prefetch as default: low disruption, small cost wins, low tail risk.
- Add an opt-in client-bundle API for high-volume micro-cadence customers (docs + SDK helper).
- For server-stitch, run a limited pilot with 2 customers, instrument stitch-hit and tail amplification (JIRA-OPS-849).
- Add a console flag per-tenant to set stitch-window (0/200/500/1000ms) and show estimated cost delta in UI.

NEXT STEPS / TODO:
- (Ethan) run 2000-user trace replay across more model sizes (7b, 13b, 34b) — capture p50/p95/p99 + cost/time breakdown. target: Apr 20
- (Priya) prototype console tickbox + cost estimate UI mock (link to mock in design PR)
- (Luca) make a small bench PR that exposes stitch-hit rate metric to observability pipeline (prometheus label: stitch_window_ms)

OPEN QUESTIONS:
- Should stitch be tenant-configurable or product-level? Default-off for hosted API and default-on for Dedicated?
- How do we present cost vs latency tradeoff to PMs and customers in plain language? Need 1-pager.
- Are there legal/billing implications if server combines multiple physical requests into one billing event? need finance signoff.

NOTES TO SELF:
- save raw bench csvs under /bench/microcadence/apr11 and attach to JIRA-OPS-849
- ping #serving-runtime with summary when pilot ready

END.
